quickAnswer: The TV Game Mode and Input Lag Tester provides a client-side visual stimulus loop to measure end-to-end response time and display latency across television panels and external monitors. It features an interactive refresh rate verification loop, statistical latency aggregation (mean, minimum, and standard deviation), and a comprehensive television picture-processing calibration guide for ALLM and VRR. All testing runs locally in browser memory.

howTo.name: Prepare Your Display
howTo.text: Connect your PC or console to your television via HDMI. Ensure Game Mode is enabled in your TV picture settings.

howTo.name: Start Latency Test
howTo.text: Click the Start Benchmark button. Watch the stage canvas for the rapid color shift.

howTo.name: Press Key on Flash
howTo.text: Press the Spacebar or click the mouse immediately when the stimulus card turns green.

howTo.name: Review Latency Stats
howTo.text: Complete 5 trials to generate your mean response time, standard deviation, and responsiveness rating.

faq.q: What is the difference between input lag and pixel response time?
faq.a: Input lag is the total delay between sending an electrical command (such as pressing a button) and the resulting action appearing on screen. Pixel response time (GtG) is merely the duration required for physical liquid crystal molecules or OLED subpixels to transition between colors. A television can have fast 1ms pixel response time but high 80ms input lag if post-processing is active.

faq.q: How does TV Game Mode reduce input lag?
faq.a: Standard television picture modes route incoming HDMI video through internal digital signal processors (DSPs) to apply noise reduction, motion smoothing (frame interpolation), dynamic contrast, and upscaling. Game Mode bypasses these processing pipelines, cutting input latency from 60ms-120ms down to under 10ms-15ms.

faq.q: What is Auto Low Latency Mode (ALLM)?
faq.a: ALLM is an HDMI 2.1 protocol feature that enables a connected console or PC to automatically command the television display to switch into low-latency Game Mode upon launching a game, and revert to normal picture mode when playing a movie.

faq.q: Why does testing at 120Hz feel more responsive than 60Hz?
faq.a: At 60Hz, a new frame is rendered every 16.67 milliseconds. At 120Hz, this interval is cut in half to 8.33 milliseconds. This 8.34ms reduction in scanout latency creates a noticeably tighter connection between user input and onscreen movement.

Game Mode Verification Checklist

  • HDMI Port Selection: Use HDMI 2.1 ports labeled 4K@120Hz or eARC for optimal bandwidth.
  • Motion Smoothing / TruMotion: Ensure frame interpolation (soap opera effect) is disabled.
  • Chroma 4:4:4: Label HDMI input as PC to bypass internal color downsampling filters.
articleHtml:
Display Input Latency and Television Picture Processing

Modern televisions are engineered primarily for broadcast video presentation and film mastering, where visual fidelity takes precedence over instantaneous response time. Configuring modern displays for interactive gaming demands eliminating digital signal processing overhead.

The Television Digital Signal Processing (DSP) Pipeline

When an HDMI signal enters a television, it typically passes through an array of temporal image processing algorithms before reaching the panel's timing controller (T-CON):

  • Temporal Motion Interpolation (MEMC): Frequently marketed as TruMotion, Auto Motion Plus, or Motionflow, these processors buffer multiple video frames in RAM to synthesize intermediary frames. This creates smooth 24 fps movie cadence but introduces 60ms to 120ms of artificial latency.
  • Local Dimming Calculation Arrays: Full-array local dimming (FALD) and Mini-LED backlights calculate regional luminance values across hundreds or thousands of backlight zones, adding 5ms to 15ms of temporal frame delay.
  • Spatial Noise Reduction and Super Resolution: Edge enhancement, compression artifact reduction, and bilinear smoothing filters buffer video frames across line stores, delaying display scanout.

Auto Low Latency Mode (ALLM) and Variable Refresh Rate (VRR)

HDMI 2.1 introduced standard signaling primitives that resolve input latency dynamically:

$$\text{Total Scanout Time} = \frac{1000}{\text{Refresh Rate (Hz)}} \implies 60\text{ Hz} = 16.67\text{ ms}, \quad 120\text{ Hz} = 8.33\text{ ms}$$

Auto Low Latency Mode (ALLM) transmits an automated infoframe over the HDMI link when a game begins, commanding the TV's system-on-chip to shut down memory-intensive DSP pipelines. Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) synchronizes display vertical scanout dynamically with GPU rendering cycles, eliminating both display tearing and the double-buffer presentation latency associated with traditional V-Sync.
